chief_complaint: muscle cramps, decreased urination, and heart palpitations after starting leukemia treatment
hpi_details: 45M with Burkitt lymphoma 24 hours post-chemotherapy presenting with hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia, and acute renal failure.
ideas: He thinks the chemotherapy medications are poisoning his kidneys or that he has become dangerously dehydrated from the treatment.
concerns: He is worried that his kidneys are permanently destroyed and that needing lifelong dialysis will prevent him from finishing his cancer treatment.
expectations: He hopes to receive intravenous fluids and medication to flush out the chemotherapy toxins and steady his racing heart.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Tumor Lysis Syndrome evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Tumor Lysis Syndrome is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes aggressive IV hydration, urate-lowering therapy, and continuous cardiac monitoring to correct the hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and hyperuricemia driving acute renal failure, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: muscle cramps, decreased urination, and heart palpitations after starting leukemia treatment
Key HPI features: 45M with Burkitt lymphoma 24 hours post-chemotherapy presenting with hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia, and acute renal failure.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 37.0C, HR 104 (irregular), BP 148/92, decreased urine output over the past 12 hours. Muscle cramping in the calves, positive Chvostek sign (facial twitching on tapping) from hypocalcemia, mild lower extremity edema. Bloods: Potassium 6.8 mEq/L, Phosphate 8.5 mg/dL, corrected Calcium 6.5 mg/dL, Uric acid 14 mg/dL, Creatinine 3.2 mg/dL (up from baseline 1.0 mg/dL), BUN elevated. ECG shows peaked T waves consistent with hyperkalemia.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Tumor Lysis Syndrome.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute kidney injury from another cause without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Palpitations or muscle cramps from hyperkalemia — risk of fatal cardiac arrhythmia.
management_principles: Continuous cardiac (telemetry) monitoring and STAT ECG given hyperkalemia; give IV calcium gluconate for cardiac membrane stabilization if ECG changes are present
Shift potassium intracellularly with insulin plus dextrose (10 units regular insulin with D50) and consider nebulized albuterol; avoid potassium-containing IV fluids
Give Rasburicase for hyperuricemia after confirming the patient is not G6PD-deficient (contraindicated in G6PD deficiency); aggressive IV normal saline hydration, avoiding phosphate-containing fluids

Hold the ACE inhibitor (Lisinopril) given hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury; obtain urgent nephrology consult for possible hemodialysis if hyperkalemia or renal failure are refractory to medical therapy
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Tumor Lysis Syndrome Post-Chemotherapy: muscle cramps, decreased urination, and heart palpitations after starting leukemia treatment. 45M with Burkitt lymphoma 24 hours post-chemotherapy presenting with hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia, and acute renal failure.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 37.0C, HR 104 (irregular), BP 148/92, decreased urine output over the past 12 hours. Muscle cramping in the calves, positive Chvostek sign (facial twitching on tapping) from hypocalcemia, mild lower extremity edema. Bloods: Potassium 6.8 mEq/L, Phosphate 8.5 mg/dL, corrected Calcium 6.5 mg/dL, Uric acid 14 mg/dL, Creatinine 3.2 mg/dL (up from baseline 1.0 mg/dL), BUN elevated. ECG shows peaked T waves consistent with hyperkalemia.
reference_soap.assessment: Tumor Lysis Syndrome (laboratory and clinical) occurring 24 hours after chemotherapy for Burkitt lymphoma, with hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia, and acute renal failure.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Continuous cardiac monitoring and STAT ECG; give IV calcium gluconate for cardiac membrane stabilization given peaked T waves. 2. Shift potassium intracellularly with insulin/dextrose (10 units regular insulin + D50) and nebulized albuterol; avoid potassium-containing fluids. 3. Give Rasburicase for hyperuricemia after confirming the patient is not G6PD-deficient. 4. Aggressive IV normal saline hydration; avoid phosphate-containing or calcium-containing fluids together to prevent calcium-phosphate precipitation. 5. Hold Lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) given hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury. 6. Urgent nephrology consult for possible hemodialysis if hyperkalemia, oliguria, or hyperphosphatemia are refractory to medical management.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Tumor Lysis Syndrome Post-Chemotherapy
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for muscle cramps, decreased urination, and heart palpitations after starting leukemia treatment
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for hematology_oncology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: Rapid death of chemo-sensitive cancer cells releases massive amounts of potassium, phosphate, and uric acid into the blood, overwhelming the kidneys and causing dangerous electrolyte derangements.
differentials: Acute kidney injury from another cause
red_flags: Palpitations or muscle cramps from hyperkalemia — risk of fatal cardiac arrhythmia
Decreased urine output — worsening renal failure

must_ask.say: How many hours or days ago did you receive your leukemia/lymphoma treatment?
Are you having any heart palpitations or an irregular heartbeat feeling?
Have you had any muscle cramps or weakness?
Has the amount of urine you're passing decreased?
How much fluid have you been drinking since your treatment?

history.answer: I've been having awful muscle cramps in my legs, my heart keeps fluttering and racing, and I've barely passed any urine today.
My heart feels like it is fluttering, racing fast, and skipping beats in a completely uneven rhythm.
I can't tap out a steady beat because the thumping jumps around and skips unpredictably.
It started gradually about four or five hours ago and hasn't let up since.
The fluttering began earlier this morning and has been going on continuously for the last four to five hours.
It started out of the blue while I was resting on the sofa; I haven't done any heavy lifting, exercise, or had caffeine.
I tried resting quietly, taking deep breaths, and drinking cool water, but nothing has slowed it down.
I felt lightheaded and dizzy when I stood up from the couch, but I haven't passed out.
I don't have sharp chest pain, but my chest feels somewhat tight and fluttery when it beats fast.
No, I haven't had any trouble with heat, excessive sweating, or unexplained weight loss before this illness.
I feel noticeably fatigued and weak all over, but I haven't had any nosebleeds, black stools, or unusual bruising.
No, I haven't had severe headaches, pale spells, or cold sweats when hungry.
I'm frightened by how my body is feeling, and I've noticed strange numbness and tingling around my mouth and in my fingers.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, sore throat, or cough recently.
I usually have a single cup of coffee in the morning but skipped it today, and I haven't had any alcohol for weeks.
No, I haven't taken any decongestants, cold medicines, diet pills, or asthma inhalers.
I received my very first chemotherapy infusion for Burkitt lymphoma yesterday morning, exactly 24 hours ago.
My calf muscles have been cramping up into painful knots, and my fingers feel stiff and twitchy.
I've barely made any urine for the past 12 hours, just a few dark drops when I tried to go.
I felt nauseated so I've only managed a few small sips of water today, and my mouth feels very parched.
I thought the strong chemo drugs from yesterday might be poisoning my system and shutting down my kidneys because I got dehydrated.
I'm terrified that my kidneys are ruined and that going on permanent dialysis will stop me from finishing my lymphoma therapy.
I'm hoping you can give me lots of IV fluids and medicine to flush this stuff out of my system and calm my heart flutter.
I have high blood pressure and slightly high cholesterol, and I was recently diagnosed with Burkitt lymphoma.
I had never been admitted to a hospital before yesterday, when I stayed for several hours to receive my chemotherapy infusion.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once every morning for my blood pressure.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink socially, maybe one beer a month at most, and haven't had a drink since my cancer diagnosis.
I work full-time as an accountant, and I live at home with my wife and two children.
My father had high blood pressure, but no one in my family had heart arrhythmias, early heart attacks, or sudden unexplained deaths.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 148/92 mmHg, pulse 104 beats per minute and irregular, temperature 37.0°C, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
The patient appears anxious and uncomfortable in mild distress, clutching his lower legs due to spasms.
Conjunctivae show mild pallor; sclerae are anicteric without injection.
The thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, with no palpable nodules or bruits.
Tachycardic rate with an irregularly irregular rhythm; S1 and S2 are normal without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Radial and pedal pulses are palpable bilaterally, tachycardic, and irregularly irregular without pulse deficit.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with vesicular breath sounds and no crackles, wheezes, or rhonchi.
Tapping lightly over the facial nerve anterior to the earlobe elicits involuntary twitching of the ipsilateral facial and lip muscles, demonstrating a positive Chvostek sign.
Mild 1+ pitting edema is present bilaterally over the pretibial areas and ankles.
Bilateral calves are visibly tense with involuntary spasms and elicit tenderness on gentle palpation.
No resting or postural hand tremor is observed, though intermittent fine twitching of perioral and finger muscles is noted.
